blocks.text: 1. Cosine Similarity

blocks.alt: Vector A and vector B produce an angle, giving a similarity score

blocks.text: Cosine similarity is the most widely used metric in modern RAG systems, and it gets the first of the three main candidates its own full treatment here.
It measures the angle between two vectors, ignoring their length entirely.
2. Isolating The Angle Alone
As covered in Similarity Metrics, cosine similarity cares only about direction, completely ignoring how long each vector is.
Two vectors pointing the same way score identically regardless of their size.
3. The Score Range Explained

blocks.alt: Negative 1 means opposite, 0 means unrelated, 1 means identical

blocks.text: Cosine similarity produces a score between negative one and positive one.
One means identical direction, zero means unrelated, and negative one means opposite.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Score","Meaning"],"rows":[["1.0","Identical direction, maximum similarity"],["0.0","Unrelated, no directional relationship"],["-1.0","Exactly opposite direction"]]}

blocks.text: 4. The Formula Piece By Piece

blocks.alt: A dot product is divided by magnitudes to produce a cosine score

blocks.text: The formula divides the dot product of two vectors by the product of their magnitudes.
That division is exactly what strips magnitude out of the comparison.
5. Why Text Embeddings Favor Cosine

blocks.alt: Text length varies but cosine ignores magnitude

blocks.text: A long chunk of text often produces a larger magnitude embedding than a short one.
As with the semantic similarity capture covered in Dense Embeddings, cosine similarity avoids penalizing chunks just for being longer.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Two chunks discussing the same topic, one a single sentence and one a full paragraph, can still score highly on cosine similarity, since only their shared direction matters, not how much text each one contains.

blocks.text: 6. Cosine Distance Versus Cosine Similarity

blocks.alt: Cosine similarity is higher when closer while cosine distance is lower when closer

blocks.text: Some systems report cosine distance instead, computed as one minus cosine similarity.
A smaller distance means a closer match, the exact opposite direction from similarity.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Mixing up cosine similarity and cosine distance inverts a ranking entirely. Sorting by cosine similarity wants the highest scores first, while sorting by cosine distance wants the lowest values first.

blocks.text: 7. Relationship To Dot Product

blocks.alt: Normalized vectors make cosine equal to dot product

blocks.text: As with normalized versus unnormalized vectors covered in Similarity Metrics, cosine similarity equals dot product once both vectors are normalized.
Some systems normalize vectors upfront and use the cheaper dot product instead.
8. Computational Efficiency
As with the computational cost across metrics covered in Similarity Metrics, computing magnitude for every comparison adds real overhead.
Precomputing and normalizing vectors once avoids repeating that work on every single query.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Cost per query"],"rows":[["Raw cosine similarity every time","Recomputes magnitude on every comparison"],["Precomputed normalized vectors","Reuses cheap dot product for every comparison"]]}

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Cosine Similarity Is The Right Metric

blocks.alt: Text embeddings of varying length point toward using cosine similarity

blocks.text: Comparing text chunks of varying length favors cosine similarity.
When magnitude actually carries meaningful signal, dot product, covered as the next topic in this module, is favored instead.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Sorting results by cosine distance in the same order as cosine similarity, inverting the ranking.
Recomputing magnitude on every single comparison instead of normalizing vectors upfront.
Assuming cosine similarity and dot product always give the same result on unnormalized vectors.
Using cosine similarity for a task where vector magnitude actually carries meaningful signal.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors, ignoring their length entirely.
It produces a score between negative one and positive one, where one means identical direction.
The formula divides the dot product of two vectors by the product of their magnitudes.
It avoids penalizing longer text chunks for having larger magnitude embeddings.
Cosine distance, computed as one minus cosine similarity, inverts the ranking direction.
Cosine similarity equals dot product once both vectors are normalized to unit length.
Precomputing normalized vectors avoids repeating magnitude calculations on every query.
It suits comparing text chunks of varying length, where direction matters more than size.
Next up: Dot Product, covering the metric that keeps magnitude in the comparison.
